Photo: Evergreen
By Charlotte Goldstone
11 November 2026
Evergreen is planning eight ad hoc Suez Canal and Bab-el-Mandeb Strait transits for its Far East–Europe services, according to Alphaliner, alongside four sailings aimed specifically at the Red Sea market.
The Taiwanese carrier’s 16,556 teu Ever Eon made its first Suez transit last weekend, on its way from Rotterdam to Singapore on the Ocean Alliance’s China Europe Shuttle (CES) service.
Three more eastbound CES transits are planned this year, and Ever Even is scheduled to make a westbound passage, reaching Suez on 12 December.
Evergreen is also preparing to restore direct Far East–Red Sea connections through its ad hoc OGRD service, deploying vessels of 7,024-9,466 teu, on a rotation including Jeddah, Sokhna, and Aqaba. The first vessel, the 7,024 teu Ever Superb , is scheduled to depart Qingdao on 14 November.
Meanwhile, Emirates Shipping Line is launching a fortnightly Central/South China-Red Sea (CRC) service, using three vessels of 2,500-4,900 teu on a fortnightly frequency, serving the same three Red Sea ports of Sokhna, Aqaba, and Jeddah, from Shanghai, Ningbo, and Nansha, with the inaugural sailing scheduled to leave Shanghai on 13 November.
The overlapping port choices highlight how the return of direct services could concentrate additional cargo at selected gateways, rather than distributing traffic evenly across the region.
However, the capacity implications could differ considerably between terminals.
DP World reported that its South Container Terminal at Jeddah handled more than 221,200 teu in July, its highest monthly throughput since operations began in 1999, following a 79% year-on-year increase in first-half volumes. The operator has also invested in additional handling equipment and is expanding capacity, preparing for further growth.
Nevertheless, Jeddah has faced operational pressure. In its September update, Expeditors reported congestion at the port, with landside delays of 10-12 days after discharge. The addition of further services could test terminal capacity, while ports receiving fewer calls risk losing traffic and utilisation.
Meanwhile, other major carriers are also progressively restoring longer-haul services through Suez. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd have confirmed that their ME1 service will return to the canal, joining six other Gemini Cooperation services already using the shorter route.
But the transition could create a second congestion risk at North Europe ports. Flexport warned, in its November European freight market update, that vessels taking the shorter route could arrive alongside ships still sailing around the Cape of Good Hope.
It forecasts arriving vessel capacity at 131% of normal levels in Week 47, with around 40% of that capacity arriving via Suez – the forwarder identified 31 containerships scheduled to arrive via Suez that week, with 61 coming via the Cape.
Flexport considers arrivals exceeding 120% of normal capacity a congestion risk, with at least three weeks forecast to breach that threshold between mid-November and January.
Rotterdam is already under pressure, with average container dwell times reaching 3.37 days in Week 42, and yard utilisation running at between 80% and 90%, according to Flexport.
While the return to shorter Suez routings could cut transit times by seven to ten days, they risk shifting operational pressure between ports rather than eliminating delays across the supply chain.

By Alex Lennane
11 November 2026
Even as forwarders and shippers lock in air cargo capacity, production setbacks and unreliable ocean services are still forcing manufacturers to pay heavily for emergency lift to meet customer deadlines.
Recent earnings disclosures from Rico Auto Industries, Netgear, and Logitech show how quickly supply problems translate into additional airfreight costs – squeezing margins and leaving companies seeking to recover the bill from customers or suppliers.
Shippers preparing next year’s freight tenders still face the risk of costly last-minute shipments, even if overall airfreight rates fall.
Rico Auto, in last week’s earnings call, disclosed a ₹400m ($4.3m) airfreight bill after longer ocean journeys and difficulties launching new components left it struggling to build sufficient inventory for programmes serving BMW and Toyota.
Chairman and CEO Arvind Kapur said US-bound shipments that normally took five to six weeks were taking 10-11 weeks, sometimes stretching to 12.
“We could not stop the lines of the customer,” he said. “We paid a very heavy price.”
Rico increased production to supply customers by air, while simultaneously rebuilding its ocean pipeline and warehouse stocks. Problems were concentrated in new iron components, whose weight compounded the cost of flying them.
But management acknowledged that disruption was only part of the explanation.
“Could we have done better? Yes, we could. We should have been more agile,” said Mr Kapur.
The company looked for contributions towards the additional airfreight expenditure, with one customer already having agreed to participate. It did not identify the customer or disclose the amount.
Rico expected the emergency air shipments to cease after this month, as ocean deliveries replenished stocks.
The alternative can be more expensive still. Siemens’ True Cost of Downtime 2024 report put the cost of an hour’s unplanned downtime at a large automotive plant at $2.3m. Chapman Freeborn’s Isidro Nuñez Oñate said last month that urgent freight requests could stem from planning errors, defective components, or transport disruption.
“Car plants run like clockwork, so it takes very little to throw everything off,” he said. “If the truck delivering parts for step four breaks down, or every windscreen needed for step ten turns out to be defective, the cars cannot move forward. Suddenly, the whole plant is at a standstill, with costs continuing to rise for every hour production remains inactive.””
Netgear, meanwhile, said a poorly executed factory transition by a manufacturing partner had constrained supplies of enterprise switches and some consumer routers.
During the company’s 4 November earnings call, CEO CJ Prober identified increased airfreight use among the factors behind a sequential decline in enterprise margins – however, those margins remained higher year on year.
The company was also discussing “appropriate commercial remedies” with the manufacturer, and transferring some products to other suppliers, although it did not specify whether that would cover the freight costs.
Netgear’s experience also demonstrates the limits of buying faster transport: its CFO said planned airfreight spending had been lower than anticipated because the expected production ramp failed to materialise.
The company forecast around 150 basis points of consolidated gross-margin pressure in Q4, primarily from rising memory costs and transportation associated with production recovery.
For Logitech, the deadline is the Christmas sales window. Its October earnings call included an allowance for 30-40 basis points of gross margin pressure from premium expedited airfreight in the December quarter to mitigate supply disruption and ensure products were available for holiday demand.
Commercial Vehicle Group also reported premium freight and overtime costs as production volumes increased, while recovering higher freight, commodity, and tariff costs from customers continued to lag the expenditure.
The emergency premium reflects how much capacity is committed before an urgent shipment reaches the market.
As DSV’s Achim Martinka explained at TIACA’s Air Cargo Forum in Miami: “Usually, our contracts are already signed for six or 12 months with the airlines. So everything which comes on a spontaneous, ad hoc basis will be even more expensive than the base load already on the aircraft.”
For shippers preparing their own tenders, buying longer-term protection also carries a cost.
“Forwarders can, of course, offer shippers 12-month deals, but given the market conditions, they would have to bake-in so much uncertainty the price becomes uncompetitive,” said Xeneta’s Niall van de Wouw.
JTD Advisory founder David Kerr argues that buyers should focus on securing capacity and examining fuel surcharge terms alongside the headline rate.
In his latest advisory, he urges buyers to “buy capacity, not rate”, and to “write fuel clauses against jet, not crude”, warning that falling crude prices may not translate into lower jet fuel costs.
Xeneta’s baseline is for airfreight rates to decline overall in 2027. It also expects some cargo that switched to air for reliability, rather than speed, to return to ocean once shipping schedules improve sustainably, most likely from the second quarter.
But that recovery remains conditional. Ocean schedule reliability from the Far East to North Europe was still around 10% in October, according to Xeneta.
For manufacturers facing immediate customer commitments, potentially cheaper freight next year offers little protection against the cost of recovering a missed deadline now.

Dodge Challenger Hellcat Redeye Drags Ford F-150 Lightning, It's Close Until It Isn't, Of Course
15 photos
Photo: Wheels / YouTube
The videographer behind the ' Wheels ' channel on YouTube recently took a detour around BMP – aka Bradenton Motorsports Park in Florida for some cool action from the FL2K competition, then got back to The Strip, then switched again to BMP, but now they’re hopefully back for good at Las Vegas Motor Speedway.
So, after the switcheroo back and forth from BMP to The Strip and back again, now it’s time to head back to the Las Vegas Motor Speedway as the videographer caught a couple of unlikely foes trying to bring honor to their respective brands – the Mopar side and the Blue Oval fam.
First, let’s meet the protagonists. In the left lane resides a defunct Ford F-150 Lightning, the battery-electric light-duty full-size pickup truck introduced by the Ford Motor Company in May 2021 as part of the fourteenth-generation Ford F-Series, not any of the SVT versions presented for the ninth and tenth iterations.
Both the commercial-grade and the retail versions of the Ford F-Series with electric power have quickly become resounding failures because of the spectacular failure to achieve the previewed sales levels – Ford was already lowering production in 2024 after abysmal 2022 and 2023 deliveries and then stopped production completely in 2025, writing it off as a bad omen and announcing a next-gen Lightning with an EREV (extended range EV) powertrain.
Meanwhile, in the right lane sits a blue Dodge Challenger identified in the video’s description as an SRT Hellcat Redeye, and the widebody muscle coupe is the impersonation of a very successful third generation for the Mopar vehicle. Sadly, Dodge stopped production in 2023 and focused solely on the new Charger with STLA Large underpinnings and Daytona EV or Sixpack inline-six Hurricane powertrains.
Anyway, it’s a nice contrast at The Strip between the silver EV truck and the dark blue muscle car with a widebody attitude. We all know that EVs can put up a great fight due to their AWD and instant torque, but the Mopar is no slouch, either, so it’s an interesting pairing.
Well, the drivers kept it interesting on the tarmac, too, at least for a while: the humongous pickup truck took off nice and fast at the green light, but the notoriously finicky Mopar didn’t hesitate and darted like an arrow in its lane, so the two of them were tied, neck and neck, as they raced past the Christmas tree.
Alas, it was close until it wasn’t, with the Dodge putting to great use that roaring 6.2-liter supercharged V8 engine and the massive Lightning unable to keep up the pace around halfway, so the Challenger slowly and steadily and inexorably drifted in front of the Ford for an ultimately comfortable win: 10.75s at 126 mph versus 12.67s at 105 mph!

New Waze Alert Now Live, Powered by Garmin Watches: Everything You Need To Know
10 photos
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution/Garmin
What was only a rumor one week ago is now official, as Garmin and Waze have confirmed a new partnership supposed to increase awareness for cyclists on the road.
Thanks to this collaboration, Waze will begin showing notifications in the places where cyclists are expected to be on the road, thanks to location data provided by Garmin Edge bike computers and Garmin smartwatches.
In other words, if you’re a cyclist and want to make sure that drivers know you’re there, you can configure your Garmin devices to send your location to the Waze app. Nearby drivers will receive a notification in the navigation app, so they can slow down before they reach the location where you’re flagged.
Here’s everything you need to know about this feature.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution How it works Garmin devices can already know where you are once you enable LiveTrack. This is a safety feature that users can enable to share their real-time location with selected contacts whenever they start an outdoor activity.
Users can let these contacts see their location on the map, with the data being broadcast through the smartphone (via the Garmin Connect app), on a live web link.
In addition to the current location, LiveTrack also shares additional information regarding the workout, such as the average pace, the elapsed time of the activity, the distance traveled, and the heart rate.
While most devices share the location data after they acquire the GPS signal through the Garmin Connect app using Bluetooth, some smartwatches also feature LTE support and can share the location data directly through the LTE connection, without using Bluetooth. These devices include the Fenix 9 Pro, the Forerunner 945 LTE, the quatix 8 Pro, the fenix 8 Pro with AMOLED and microLED, and the D2 Mach 2 Pro.
However, Waze users will only see the location of the cyclist on the map, without additional information being imported. Furthermore, no personal details are revealed, so the only thing that’s displayed is a cyclist icon in the place where the Garmin device was located and a notification on the screen reading “Cyclist ahead.”
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution The supported devices Garmin does not provide and maintain a list of devices that support LiveTrack, but the company specifically mentions EDGE bike computers and smartwatches as being compatible with the new Waze feature.
Theoretically, all Fenix models that are still being serviced should be able to work with LiveTrack, as well as Instinct smartwatches and the luxury models in the Marq lineup. If you’re not sure if LiveTrack is available for your device, the easiest way to figure this out is to open the Garmin Connect app, tap the More icon in the bottom-right corner, and expand the Safety & Tracking section.
If LiveTrack is there, this means that your device should be able to share your location while cycling, assuming you have already configured this feature.
As for Waze, you need to be running the latest version of the app on Android or iPhone. Android Auto and CarPlay are also supported, but at this point, there’s no word as to whether Garmin and Waze want to bring the same information to cars with Google built-in.
Photo: Bogdan Popa/autoevolution How to set up the feature If you ride your bike on public roads regularly and you already own a compatible Garmin device, you need to configure LiveTrack to share the location data with Waze.
To do this, you must install the latest version of the Garmin Connect app from your app store - LiveTrack requires at least version 5.20.
Once you are there, you must open the app and tap the More button in the lower part of the screen. Look for Safety & Tracking and tap LiveTrack. Follow the wizard on the screen to complete the setup - you’ll be prompted to define the contacts you want to allow to track you and configure how notifications will be sent. For text messages, you’ll need to pay for a Garmin Connect+ subscription.
When everything is complete, you should see a new section called Waze Location Sharing. You’ll also need to set up this feature, but the wizard shouldn’t require more than a couple of seconds to complete. Once this feature is enabled, drivers should start to see your location on the map when you start cycling on a public road, acquire a GPS signal, and activate LiveTrack.
Keep in mind that you’ll need to have your phone in your pocket or backpack (unless your Garmin device is fitted with LTE) and have a good cellular signal to be able to share your location in real time. The location data is automatically removed when you end the workout, so you will no longer be visible on Waze.
Google insists on the privacy part of the feature, explaining sharing the data with Waze is “completely opt-in and built with privacy in mind.” The company explains that the alert appearing on Waze screens is just temporary.

STUTTGART, Germany – Cellcentric’s newest fuel cell BZA375 fits in the engine bay of a 13-liter diesel truck. The plant where they are currently manufactured is located in Esslingen (in the greater Stuttgart area). The factory meant to build it at scale is being prepared. For now it sits as a reserved plot in an industrial park in the town of Weilheim an der Teck, Germany.
The joint venture of Daimler Truck and Volvo Group won’t build there until Europe has truck-sized hydrogen stations and fuel near €6 (about $6.70) per kilogram , so that end customers can operate fuel cell electric trucks, which have been proven in practice, in a cost-effective manner, its chief technology officer said. That leaves the timing of hydrogen trucking at scale with fuel suppliers, station builders and governments.
Nicholas Loughlan, cellcentric’s CTO, laid out that plan during a Sept. 17 media visit to the company’s headquarters in Kirchheim/Teck, near Stuttgart.
“You cannot just put a product out there and expect it to scale,” Loughlan said. “You need a whole ecosystem and infrastructure and a whole framework for it to work.”
The visit came two days after Daimler Truck, Volvo, Toyota, Bosch and four energy companies formed an alliance at IAA Transportation to roll out hydrogen stations in step with truck fleets, starting in Germany. In July, Toyota signed a binding agreement to become an equal one-third owner of cellcentric, with closing expected around year-end or early 2027.
One fuel cell replaces two
The BZA150, cellcentric’s current system, powers a 40-metric-ton truck with two 150-kilowatt units. The company stopped it short of full series production and fast-tracked its successor BZA375, Loughlan said.
The BZA375, unveiled in April 2026, delivers up to 375 kW of continuous net power, more than 500 horsepower, from a single unit weighing less than 500 kilograms, about 1,100 pounds. cellcentric rates it at less than 6 kilograms of hydrogen per 100 kilometers in a fully loaded 40-ton truck, or more than 10.2 miles per kilogram, with a service life of about 25,000 hours.
“We do our homework, too,” Loughlan said. “That’s why BZA375 uses 20% less fuel than the BZA150 twin system.”
During the visit, cellcentric said BZA375 also fits North American tractors such as the Volvo VNL and Freightliner Cascadia, along with Europe’s Mercedes-Benz Actros and Volvo FH.
Esslingen builds now, Weilheim waits
The Esslingen pilot plant, about 30 kilometers from headquarters, has handled every production step under one roof since June 2024. The line is building BZA150s for customer fleets that reach operators starting at the end of this year and will move to increased sample production of the BZA375, Loughlan said. Series production of the BZA375 is planned for the turn of the decade.
Weilheim is the second step. cellcentric holds an option until the end of 2029 on 16 hectares, about 40 acres, in Weilheim’s Rosenloh industrial park, and Loughlan confirmed it paid more than €15 million (about $16.8 million) to reserve the land.
“We’re not investing into a huge manufacturing facility in the first place, knowing how, let’s say, the transformation of new technology is sometimes difficult to manage, as we all know,” he said.
No order count triggers construction. Loughlan said the decision rests on how far cellcentric can push Esslingen’s output and how fast demand builds, and a new plant takes “three to four years, as always.”
“There’s not a specific timing and also not a specific number for us,” he said. “It’s more a how do we judge market dynamic.”
The grid case for a second network
Loughlan’s argument for hydrogen starts with the power grid. Running Europe’s entire in-use truck fleet on batteries would take about 500 terawatt-hours of electricity, he said, “roughly the energy consumption that Germany has in a year.”
“That can be done technically, but economically, from a timing perspective and realistic implementation, that probably is not a smart move,” he said.
Germany produced 509.2 TWh in 2025, according to Destatis’ gross electricity production series , and ACEA counts 6.2 million trucks – of which approximately 3.9 million are heavy-duty trucks weighing more than 16 metric tons – in use across the EU.
In an example, trucks fill the lot at the Denkendorf service station on the A8 autobahn near Stuttgart at the end of a shift, Loughlan said, showing an aerial view. The stop has no charger built for trucks today, and planning calls for a 15.4-megawatt grid connection there by 2035, enough for about 15 trucks to megawatt-charge at once, he said.
Energy providers are already telling customers who want new connections for industry or long-haul trucking that they can’t upgrade the grid fast enough, according to Loughlan. That is where building “two infrastructures for heavy-duty becomes a lot more practical, a lot cheaper, and a lot more effective,” he said, adding that electrification should still happen wherever possible.
Stations sized for trucks, fuel priced for fleets
EU rules already set a floor for hydrogen stations. The Alternative Fuels Infrastructure Regulation requires stations of at least 1 metric ton a day with a 700-bar dispenser every 200 kilometers along the core TEN-T road network, plus one in each urban node, by Dec. 31, 2030. cellcentric’s slides call for heavy-duty station designs scalable to 4 metric tons a day.
Europe has 187 hydrogen stations, Daimler Truck CEO Karin Rådström said at IAA, and most dispense at 350 bar. Important to know: These are mainly passenger car refueling stations – not suited for HD trucks with a fuel demand >10 kg at 700 bar or liquid hydrogen.
Price is the wider gap.
“If we can get six euros per kilogram for hydrogen price, we’re okay to start scaling,” Loughlan said. Asked the current price in Europe, he said, “Substantially higher.”
In January, H2 Mobility began selling hydrogen to customers of truck rental firm hylane for about €8 (about $9) per kilogram net at selected German stations, a price the companies said was well below current market levels .
Loughlan credited Germany’s funding program for tying station money to truck deployments. “So we solve the chicken and egg equation,” he said. Germany’s latest call offered €220 million (about $247 million), and applicants requested more than 70 high-capacity stations and 800 heavy-duty trucks, according to the alliance .
The regulatory pressure lands on truck makers. Under the EU’s heavy-duty CO2 standards , new heavy-duty vehicles must cut CO2 per kilometer 45% by 2030 and 65% by 2035.
“It’s an OEM legislation that’s not an end customer legislation,” Loughlan said. “That means the customer will choose the best technology for this job and what’s the best TCO.”
What the fuel cell hasn’t solved
cellcentric’s timelines have slipped before. When Volvo agreed in 2020 to pay €600 million, almost $700 million at the time, for half the venture, the partners planned series production for the second half of this decade. First systems were originally due from Weilheim in 2026, and cellcentric now expects operations there “around 2030,” citing slow hydrogen infrastructure and the price of green hydrogen, Electrive reported .
Cost still depends on volume. “If you don’t produce tens of thousands every year, then, of course, your cost position is not where it can be,” Loughlan said, adding that the early stage needs government support.
He said Toyota will bring experience industrializing fuel cells at scale in passenger cars such as the Mirai.
In North America, cellcentric is holding back, even though Loughlan said the system was developed with U.S. and Canadian codes and standards in mind.
“There’s currently, our assessment at least, not a huge, let’s say, demand for zero-emission trucking in the U.S. right now,” he said. “So we’ve taken a bit of a more observing position.”
Loughlan said stations, fuel price and cellcentric’s own volume have to grow together before fleets commit.
“And then the end customers will go, ‘I’m not only buying one for show purposes, I’m going to buy 10,'” he said.
Why it matters: cellcentric’s BZA375 fits a 13-liter diesel bay and cuts fuel use 20% from its predecessor, but series production waits until the turn of the decade. Whether its Weilheim plant gets built depends on truck-sized stations and hydrogen near €6 per kilogram. Operators will then be able to use heavy-duty fuel-cell trucks for long-haul transport, with overall TCO-comparable to those of diesel trucks.

2026 EICMA's Speed Legends Exhibit Was Not To Be Missed – See the Bikes That Paved MotoGP History
31 photos
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution
Autoevolution recently received an invitation to EICMA. How could we resist?! While we didn’t know all of what we would witness at the event, one exhibition we stumbled across was designed to take us through the years of MotoGP racing heritage and bring us up to speed. Here’s what we witnessed.
EICMA is the largest two-wheeler and motorcycle event in the world, spanning over 3.5 million square feet and hosting close to and sometimes, exceeding 800,000 visitors over the course of just six days. It’s here that we found the Speed Legends exhibition that occupied a corner of Hall 22 of the event.
When you first lock eyes with Speed Legends, you do so from behind the exhibit, signaled by orange and black pillars that block out most of the view inside . Secondly, you’re drawn to the insanely large queue that snakes around the exterior of the show. As press, I was able to skip this line, and what I found inside required that I captured most, if not, all of the bikes.
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution Over 30 iconic rides were on display, and the first to kick off the experience was a 500cc AJS Porcupine on loan from Sammy Miller Museum. It stood alone under the spotlight and in the center of the space while the remaining rides all stood around as if to look at where it all began.
This year, the EICMA Speed Legends was focused on 500cc wonders, with an exception or two here and there.
As for the rest of the bikes, the other “first one” was an 8-cylinder Motto Guzzi from 1955 with a weight of 137 kg (302 lbs) and top speed of 285 kph (177 mph). It was tamed by Ken Kavanagh but had zero race wins. Maybe it’s the fact that it looks like a bullet with two wheels that it made the show. Maybe it was the top speed.
Up next, MV Agusta made its presence with a 1958 6-cylinder beast with a weight of 180 kg (397 lbs), but no mentioned top speed, this time, ridden by John Hartle. I’m loving that sky blue monocoque fairing with red winds. A Cola-red backside pops against the whole thing too.
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution Names like Norton would make their appearance, with a 1960 Manx with 22 race winds according to the exhibition and a top speed of 230 kph (143 mph). It only weighs 140 kg (309 lbs). What you need to consider about this little crotch rocket is that it was rocking a single-cylinder engine. Think about that; one cylinder!
A Gilera made its appearance too, from 1963 and sporting a 69 hp engine with 4 cylinders and a top speed of 260 kph (161 mph). It racked up 34 wins according to Speed Legends. Another 4-cylinder was Benelli’s Quatro with its green, grey, yellow livery and an undisclosed top speed with 91 ponies carrying a 147 kg (324 lbs) weight.
As we step into years like 1970, we start to see names like Kawasaki come to light, with a 3-cylinder in-line H1-R with 74 stallions pushing a 134 kg (295 lbs) body along. Christian Ravel drove this one and it was present from Eric de Seynes collection.
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution Once 1971 started to roll around, Ducati would see its name in the 500cc category, with a twin-cylinder, 72 hp two-wheeler weighing just 138 kg (304 lbs). Top speed sat at 250 kph (155 mph). MV Agusta was up next with a three-cylinder with 62 race wins and a top speed of 230 kph (142 mph). Clearly, speed isn’t everything.
But, very few names stood out quite like the 67 hp Paton 500 with 250 kph (155 mph) top speed, standing as the placeholder of 1973. It carried no race wins, so I'm trying to figure out the criteria for the choices here.
For 1974, MV Agusta would be back on the Speed Legends podium with a four-cylinder monster with 97 hp and a top speed of 290 kph (180 mph) at just 140 kg (308 lbs). Phil Read is the pilot showcased at the top of this ride’s plaque.
1975 would be represented with a Yamaha OW 23 with a 99 hp output and top speed of 290 kph, showcased in red and white with a yellow “number plate.” It looked quite Lucky Strike.
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution What I noticed during the show is that the 70s brought with them a different fairing styling. Brands seemed to understand that, while the teardrop is a great aerodynamic shape, racing is down to control, and the body could clearly be improved or manipulated to handle differently based on needs and speeds.
The 1977 Suzuki XR22 was the bike where this transition was most obvious at the Speed Legends exhibit. More horsepower was also no being offered, with the XR22 coming in with 112 , around 15% more than previous decades.
Another Suzuki followed 1977, under 1982, and was able to produce 133 hp and capping at 280 kph (173 mph) with a weight of 121 kg (267 lbs). It was a four-cylinder ridden by Franco Uncini and is even part of his collection.
For 1986, we we’re granted a view of an Elf 3, 1986 represented by a Yamaha YZR OW86, and for 1990, we finally got to see the Lucky Strike livery in a Suzuki RGV 500 XR76 with a top speed of 324 kph (201 mph) and 167 hp at just 115 kg (253 lbs). It brought home 36 wins. Rothman’s 1991 Honda NSR500 was next.
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution One name I had never heard of was Cagiva, representing 1993 with a C593 that could max out at 310 kph (193 mph) with 185 ponies. Aprilia made its appearance for 2003, with an RS Cube, which, according to Speed Legends, was a 1,000cc ride, so it broke the mold of the exhibition, but it wasn’t alone.
The blue Yamaha YZF-M1 from 2004 was also a 1,000cc ride, and for 2006 too, more 1,000 goodness in the form of a Ducati Desmosedici GP06.
But, Speed Legends also brought in some oddball engine capacities, one of which was in the form of a Ilmor X3 with 800 ccs cranking out 217 hp and a top speed of 315 kph (196 mph). A Kawasaki ZX-RR with 800 cc stood alongside the Ilmor, and next to that, a Desmosedici GP08.
Two more Yamaha YZF-M1s hop on the 800 CC category which is soon broken by the presence of a Honda RC213V bearing the Repsol livery.
Photo: Cristian Curmei | Autoevolution Finally, we start to see none other than Red Bull in the mix, strapped to a KTM RC16 with 261 hp and a top speed of 350 kph (217 mph) ridden by Pol Espargaró in 2018.
The last two podiums belonged to none other than Yamaha, with a YZF-M1 for 2021, rocking a 1,000cc engine, and ridden by Fabio Quartararo and showcasing the Monster livery, and for 2022, another Desmosedici GP22 that was rocked by Pecco Bagnaia and showcasing 90 wins according to the EICMA event.
Now, I'll be honest, stepping into the Speed Legends event, I had no idea what to expect, and I’m so glad that I chose to step in there. Why? Well, not having the strongest backgorund in motorcycles of its history, the event stood as a perfect stage where we could see how the industry moved from its early beginnings through to what it is today, or rather yesterday: 2022.
Simply put, I was able to witness the progression of the game, and it helped me grasp just how serious things have become, and countless folks at the event are sure to have felt the same. Enjoy the show below.

1970 Plymouth Satellite "Superbird" Was $100K, Buyer Drove 3,000 Miles, Asks 145k Six Months Later
68 photos
Photo: Chrome Cars
Chrysler engineers spent thousands of hours inside wind tunnels during 1969 to make the 1970 Plymouth Road Runner Superbird splice the atmosphere at 200 mph, which meant a folding fabric roof was completely out of the question. Yet, sitting inside the Phoenix showroom of Streetside Classics in Mesa, Arizona, is the ultimate Mopar contradiction: a 1970 Plymouth B-body with a nose cone, a rear wing, and no roof in between them. It’s a Bird? It’s a plane? No, it’s not Superbird/man, but a Satellite.
In period NASCAR competition, a hypothetical drag-inducing soft top would have shredded at high speed, and the towering rear wing was specifically engineered to brace against rigid quarter panels above a flush-mounted rear window plug. This custom build embraces that mechanical paradox with a pointed nose cone, concealed headlights, front fender air extractors, exposed chrome hood pins, white side strobes, and a black vinyl top fitted with a glass rear window.
Beneath the pinned hood sits a non-original 440-cubic-inch V8 upgraded with Indy aluminum cylinder heads and a Holley four-barrel carburetor, coupled via an A727 TorqueFlite 3-speed automatic transmission to an 8.75-inch rear axle. The chassis features Hotchkis suspension, tubular upper control arms, subframe connectors, drilled and slotted front disc brakes, Dynomax dual exhaust, 15-inch Rallye wheels on 275/60R15 BFGoodrich tires, and a white vinyl bucket-seat interior with a console.
To understand the hows and whys circumvoluting the very existence of this open-air aero warrior wannabe, let’s glance at the humble B-body platform that donated its bones: the Plymouth Satellite. Introduced for the 1965 model year and produced across three distinct generations through 1974, the Satellite debuted as the flagship trim of the intermediate Belvedere line – the rootstock on which all Plymouth mid-sizer scions were grafted in the sixties.
Photo: Chrome Cars First-generation models ran from 1965 to 1967 and were offered strictly as two-door hardtops and convertibles equipped with standard vinyl bucket seats.
The second generation spanned 1968 to 1970, expanding the Satellite into a family series with four-door sedans, station wagons, and the upscale Sport Satellite sub-series, before the fuselage-styled third generation carried the badge from 1971 until the mid-size Fury replaced it in 1975. While this family tree would induce the impression that the Satellite was mostly a grocery getter, the moniker has some very high-horse rights to sit among the legendary Mopar muscle cars .
The most potent factory-badged Satellite ever built was the 1966 Street Hemi variant, packing a 426-cubic-inch dual-quad V8 rated at 425 horsepower and 490 lb-ft of torque. Mother Mopar’s emblematic powerhouse wasn’t only for Road Runners and Coronets (the two monikers to sport the most abundant production numbers of the nefarious big-block), but also for Satellites and Belvederes. At least, that’s what it was in the beginning.
Photo: Chrome Cars After Plymouth spun off the big-block GTX in 1967 and the budget-minded Road Runner in 1968, the Satellite focused on mainstream versatility, recording 82,654 total units for the 1970 model year. Not too bad, considering the total mid-size production of 158,000 units for the cheapest ChryCo division at the debut of the seventies.
Standard RH-series Satellite domestic deliveries comprised 38,129 four-door sedans, 28,200 two-door hardtops, 4,204 six-passenger station wagons, 3,277 nine-passenger station wagons, and just 701 two-door convertibles, while the upscale RP-series Sport Satellite added 8,749 hardtops, 3,010 sedans, and 3,624 wagons. In other words, the one-of-zero example you see in the gallery is built on the rarest Plymouth body style of them all for 1970. It’s something.
That year, Satellite buyers could choose between a standard 145-horsepower 225-cube Slant Six with a single-barrel carburetor, a 230-horsepower 318 two-barrel V8, a 290-horsepower 383-CID two-barrel V8, or a top-spec 330-horsepower 383-cubic-inch four-barrel V8. Transmission choices included a standard 3-speed manual, an optional 4-speed manual, or a 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic.
Photo: Chrome Cars A 1970 Satellite convertible carried a base price of $2,970 with the Slant Six or $3,060 with the standard-issue 318 V8.
Conversely, the 1970 Plymouth Road Runner Superbird occupied the opposite end of the Mopar spectrum, engineered to satisfy NASCAR homologation rules and lure Richard Petty back to the Plymouth camp from Ford.
Unlike the multi-variant Satellite, the Superbird was offered in a single RM23 two-door hardtop body style topped by a mandatory vinyl roof to conceal the rear window plug welds, carrying a factory base price of $4,298 before options.
When NASCAR raised its homologation requirement from 500 cars to one unit per two Plymouth dealers for 1970, the division produced at least 1,935 Superbirds. Every example packed a big-block V8 paired with either a 4-speed manual or a 3-speed TorqueFlite automatic, resulting in 824 manuals and 1,084 automatic transmissions installed across the domestic run.
Photo: Chrome Cars At the base of the Superbird hierarchy sat the U-code 375-horsepower 440-4 Super Commando V8, which accounted for 1,084 cars split between 626 TorqueFlite automatics and 458 manuals.
Next came the V-code 390-horsepower 440 Six-Barrel V8 with three twos (two-barrel carburetors) at 716 units, comprising 408 automatics and 308 three-pedals, while the 425-horsepower R-code 426-cubic-inch Street Hemi totaled 135 cars: 77 automatics and 58 row-your-owns.
With authentic hardtop Superbirds commanding steep six-figure, and exceptional examples going into seven figures, and an open-air factory version never having existed, a builder decided to merge Plymouth's rarest 1970 B-body drop-top with its wildest aero package . According to its VIN, (RH27C0G208913) this car rolled off the St. Louis, Missouri assembly line in 1970 as one of those 701 Satellite convertibles, originally equipped with a C-code 225-cubic-inch Slant-Six engine under the hood.
Photo: Chrome Cars Swapping that economy-oriented six-cylinder for a 440-cubic-inch V8 and grafting on the winged nose-and-tail kit birthed this custom tribute, which shows 42,187 miles on the odometer, and $144,995 on its asking price tag. Asan added curiosity, note that this car offered for sale (and subsequently sold) earlier this year by a German dealership , with an asking price of €89,000 (about $99k), and with 39,916 miles on the clock.
According to the German listing, the wing comes from an original Superbird, and the fenders are also original (they didn’t specify which fenders, namely the ones holding the wing, or the front ones). Rest of the Superbird lookalike details (nose cone, pop-up headlights, air scoops are reproductions crafted by a Superbird specialist.
I know some would consider it a blasphemy, while other, more understanding gearheads will appreciate the workmanship. Which side are you one? There’s a comment section for that answer, feel free to use it.

Refreshed 2028 Kia EV9 Large All-Electric Crossover SUV Shines Brightly in CGI, Both Inside and Out
25 photos
Photo: AutoYa / YouTube
Kia America is enjoying a great time in recent years across the US automotive market. The most recent novelties also attest to that, with the 2027 Telluride Hybrid named “Favorite Family Vehicle” at Midwest Automotive Media Association’s (MAMA) Fall Fest or the 2027 EV3 inducted as the “Best EV” by the Western Automotive Journalists (WAJ) at Best of the Bay 2026.
However, more importantly, the company has a solid lineup, and for six consecutive months Kia America has achieved record-breaking sales across the US automotive market. In October alone, sales rose by 16% to 80k units, while no less than eight models rocked “significant year-over-year sales growth,” including V9 (+111 percent); Telluride (+63%); EV6 (+58%); Seltos (+43%); Sorento (+31%); Carnival (+17%); K4 (+14%); and Sportage (+12%).
Telluride, Sportage HEV, and Carnival HEV delivered best-ever monthly sales records, and year-to-date, Kia has sold in America no less than 747,394 units compared to 705,150 deliveries last year. Interestingly, the sales of the Kia EV9 flagship all-electric model continue to rise, although the US automotive market has turned a blind eye toward EVs recently.
As such, it’s no wonder the rumor mill believes that Kia will soon update the battery-electric mid-size crossover SUV with three-row seating made by Kia in South Korea and especially at West Point, Georgia (KMMG) in America since 2023. More precisely, the good folks over at the " AutoYa " info channel on YouTube have unofficially imagined the CGI look of the facelifted 2028 Kia EV9 model with help from their resident virtual artist, a member of the imaginative guild of digital car content creators.
According to the channel’s host, the all-electric three-row seven-seater Kia EV9 has been around since 2024 across North America, and they think it's time to update the model with a mid-cycle facelift in 2027, most likely for the 2028 model year. The facelift could bring an exterior refresh, subtle interior changes, as well as better technology with larger-capacity battery packs for all versions.
With help from their resident pixel master, they also spent some time illustrating all the possible CGI changes for the new Kia EV9, both inside and outside – and also added a ton of ritzy color options both for the exterior and the interior. On the outside, the changes are mostly visible up front, as the rear only gets updated LED taillight graphics: a new placement of the LED headlights in the bumper, with the vertical LED array now dedicated solely to the DRLs.
Inside, on the other hand, the changes are way subtler: we can see the same dashboard layout, but now the CGI expert has envisioned the 2028 Kia EV9 with a new three-spoke wheel and with physical controls below the 12.3-inch central infotainment screen. So, what do you think – yay or nay?

VIENNA — Hackers linked to Russia’s FSB quietly compromised a Romanian government organization’s servers to collect emails related to NATO and the EU in December 2025, a Slovak cybersecurity firm has revealed.
Using an advanced suite of tools that the researchers dubbed Cereal, a pun on the technology of serialization, emails going through Romanian government servers were scanned for a relation to NATO and the European Union. If this was discovered, the malicious software would create a copy for its Russian spymasters.
In particular, one component, CerealBox, targeted messages involving NATO and EU institutional addresses, the cybersecurity form ESET said. The module selected emails with Word or PDF attachments using predefined filters, then compressed and encrypted copies for later retrieval by the attackers.
The hack was discovered by the Bratislava-based company and made public on Nov. 10. ESET had first discovered the tool being used against Kazakhstan in November 2025, and found the infiltration of Romania’s Microsoft Exchange servers a month later.
In a blog post and press release, the company attributed the attack to the known hacking group Turla, which it said was generally considered to be affiliated with Russia’s FSB, the country’s domestic intelligence agency. Turla has also been involved in attacks against high-profile Ukrainian targets, and the researchers said 70% of countries the group targeted were post-Soviet or post-communist states in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. The APT – a term designating an “Advanced Persistent Threat,” or known hacking group – primarily attacks government institutions.
ESET attributed the toolset to Turla with high confidence, citing the simultaneous use of another component publicly linked to the group and conceptual similarities to older Turla malware.
The researchers also noted a surge in activity in Kazakhstan on Jan. 15, 2026, the day after Old New Year, an informal holiday observed in Russia and some neighboring countries. “While malware does not celebrate holidays, its operators do,” the company wrote.
Romanian servers were compromised on Dec. 23, 2025, ESET researchers said; roughly a month after the cybersecurity firm first detected the same malicious code on the server of a Kazakh government agency. That discovery was the first time this tool had been seen, which the researchers described as “a previously undocumented toolset: a collection of modular .NET malware designed to run on Microsoft Exchange servers, receive commands, execute them in memory, map the compromised organization, and collect selected email messages.”
The tool was unusual for its “combination of novel techniques requiring deep knowledge of Exchange internals with unusual .NET execution methods,” ESET wrote.
The tool was designed to be especially stealthy, meant to allow it to spy undetected at length. While malware commonly communicates with an external command-and-control server, which can lead to detection and help cybersecurity professionals trace the origin, Cereal used the target organization’s own Microsoft servers as its infrastructure.
Romania is an eastern flank member of NATO and has faced physical and digital spillover of the confrontation between Russia and the West, particularly since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. Airspace violations, drone shootdowns and even the strike of commercial vessels in its exclusive economic zone have been among the consequences.
The country has also been targeted by cyber warfare. In May 2025, another known Russian APT actor attacked arms makers involved in supporting Ukraine, including those located in Romania; and just months after the war broke out, government websites were hit by a crude distributed denial-of-service attack, making Romanian public-authority and financial-sector websites unavailable for several hours.

By: Northern Miner Staff November 11, 2026
The second instalment of our U.S. exploration spotlight features four juniors testing whether early drill results point to deposits with room to grow. In Arizona, Prismo Metals is looking beneath an old silver camp for a copper system. Relevant Gold is testing two targets in Wyoming, Ridgeline Minerals is tracing a silver-rich discovery in Nevada and Tectonic Metals is working towards an initial gold resource in Alaska.
Prismo Metals
Prismo Metals (CSE: PRIZ; US-OTC: PMOMF) is testing whether its historical Silver King silver project, about 110 km east of Phoenix, sits above a concealed porphyry copper system.
Mapping expanded the alteration footprint to about 2.1 by 2.4 km, Prismo reported in September. The core of potassic alteration, which can occur in the hotter central parts of porphyry systems, more than doubled to about 650 by 300 metres. The company used mapping, sampling, geophysics and initial drilling to refine its model.
Drill hole SK-26-08 cut 21.5 metres grading 0.4 gram gold per tonne, 94 grams silver, 0.28% copper and 0.21% lead from 47.3 metres depth, Prismo reported in June. The next test is whether the silver veins and breccias connect to a larger copper system below the old workings.
Silver King produced nearly 6 million oz. of silver between 1875 and 1889, and another 230,999 oz. between 1918 and 1928. Prismo optioned the project in 2025. It also has an indirect interest in Arizona’s Hot Breccia copper project through its 24% stake in Blade Resources (CSE: AZCU). Vizsla Silver (TSX: VZLA; NYSE-A: VZLA) holds a 5% stake in Prismo.
Prismo Metals had a market value of about C$5 million at print time.
Relevant Gold
Relevant Gold (TSXV: RGC; US-OTC: RGCCF) is drilling Bradley Peak and Lewiston in central Wyoming to test whether a little-explored belt of Archean rocks can host a gold district.
The company started a 5,000- to 7,000-metre drill program in July at Bradley Peak, about 218 km northwest of Cheyenne, after receiving an expanded five-year exploration permit from the U.S. Bureau of Land Management. Work initially focused on Apex, one of six prospects at Bradley Peak and the only one drilled before this year.
All 12 drill holes in last year’s Apex program intersected anomalous gold over about 600 metres of strike, although grades were low and intervals narrow. This year’s work is testing whether those structures persist and host higher-grade shoots. The company’s model draws on Archean gold camps in Canada, where large deposits can be associated with deep crustal structures.
Relevant began another 5,000-metre drill program in August at the Burr target on its Lewiston project in the historical South Pass gold camp. Kinross Gold (TSX: K; NYSE: KGC) and investors William Bollinger and Rob McEwen participated in a C$15-million financing this year. Neither Wyoming project has a resource estimate.
Relevant Gold had a market value of about C$49 million at print time.
Ridgeline Minerals
Ridgeline Minerals (TSXV: RDG; US-OTC: RDGMF) sold four Nevada gold properties to Nevada Gold Mines for $23.2 million in cash in August. The sale gives Ridgeline capital to pursue early discoveries, while South32 (ASX, LSE, JSE: S32) funds exploration at the Selena silver-zinc-lead-gold project under an earn-in agreement.
Ridgeline’s silver-zinc-lead-gold Selena project in east-central Nevada. Credit: Ridgeline Metals
At Selena, earlier drilling in the Chinchilla zone cut 32.5 metres grading 153.42 grams silver per tonne, 2.51% lead, 1.6% zinc and 0.09 gram gold from 235 metres vertical depth. In the Juniper zone, drill hole LB-072 returned 7.7 metres at 725.2 grams silver, 1.5 grams gold, 1.3% lead and 0.9% zinc from 15.5 metres depth.
Ridgeline is using geophysics, mapping and drilling to test whether those intercepts belong to a broader carbonate replacement system. Selena lies about 1 km west of the Butte Valley porphyry and skarn project, which Ridgeline interprets as the source of the fluids that mineralized its property.
South32 can earn 60% of Selena by spending at least $10 million over an initial five-year term and increase its interest to 80% by spending another $10 million. Ridgeline remains the operator and also holds the Coyote gold and Big Blue copper-gold projects in Nevada.
Ridgeline Minerals had a market value of about C$33 million at print time.
Tectonic Metals
Tectonic Metals (TSXV: TECT; US-OTC: TETOF) is targeting an initial gold resource in the first quarter of 2027 at Chicken Mountain, the most advanced target at its Flat project in southwestern Alaska. Drilling is also testing Black Creek, a second centre of gold mineralization about 6 km northeast.
At Chicken Mountain, drill hole CMD26-036 cut 30 metres grading 1.4 grams gold per tonne from 183 metres depth, Tectonic reported in September. A deeper interval returned 118.1 metres at 0.51 gram gold from 270 metres to the end of the drill hole. The results extended one of six higher-grade corridors to more than 300 metres vertical depth.
At Black Creek, drilling reported in August cut 21.3 metres at 5.09 grams gold, including 6.1 metres at 17.34 grams. Another drill hole returned 57.9 metres at 1.89 grams gold. Both ended in mineralization. The results followed last year’s first drilling at Black Creek, which cut 48.77 metres at 4.5 grams gold from surface.
Tectonic launched a roughly 40,000-metre program in May to support the Chicken Mountain estimate and test other targets. Flat covers about 404 sq. km, mainly on land owned by Alaska Native regional corporation Doyon, one of Tectonic’s largest shareholders. The property lies about 40 km northeast of the Donlin gold project.
Tectonic Metals had a market value of about C$241 million at print time.

If you were wondering about General Motors and what it’s been up to recently, we heard that the company has finally relented to hybrid peer pressure, and after watching Japanese and Korean automakers gain massive ground with their electrified models, they are finally ready to crave a piece of the HEV pie.
GM spent years building a cult for EV models, and now America is waging war against zero-emission vehicles and their sales are, naturally, nosediving. So, a change of scenery was in order, and after carmakers like Toyota or Kia profited massively from the current hybrid boom, the biggest of the US automakers will join the fray with three hybrid sport utility vehicles, namely the HEV options for the Chevrolet Traverse, GMC Acadia, and Buick Enclave , according to a report from Reuters.
But even if that’s very interesting, we’re actually here to discuss an even larger SUV – the GMC Yukon, as an example that was thoroughly customized to stand out in any crowd was recently shared on social media by the good folks over at Miami, Florida-based Vossen . They have gotten their hands on a batch of cool pictures featuring another GM - this time around a Yukon AT4- after not long ago we saw them showcase a GMC Sierra HD Denali on Gloss Black Vossen HFX-5 wheels.
The company promises that the new Vossen HFX-5 alloys will make a statement, and they continue with this silver-over-black GMC Yukon AT4 that has loads of Gloss Black details, including the new set of rims, which are shod in massive all-terrain tires. The Vossen HFX-5 are hybrid forged alloy wheels offered in both a six-lug or eight-lug configuration, with the former present on the mighty full-size body-on-frame SUV.
The prices kick off at $525 for each wheel, and the options are 17 through 24-inch diameters with 8.5- to 12-inch widths and a ton of colorful finishes. Of course, the owner chose Gloss Black for the wheels to mix and match with other trim elements of the SUV. Otherwise, if you’re interested in buying a brand-new GMC Yukon of the refreshed fifth-generation variety, you’ll need a 2027 model year before thinking that the sky is the limit when it comes to customization options from the aftermarket realm.
So, a 2027 GMC Yukon kicks off at an MSRP of no less than $70,200 sans destination, with available seating for up to eight people, and the AT4 is 4WD only starting from $80,695 with the 5.3-liter V8 engine and a ten-speed automatic transmission. Of course, you can always change the powertrain to the 6.2-liter V8 or the 3.0-liter Duramax turbo diesel – maybe for the next model year GM will introduce the new 5.7-liter and 6.6-liter V8s from the Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra on their Chevy Tahoe and GMC Yukon cousins, too. source_document.body:
Some shippers are heading into peak season with the bid strategy that carried them from 2022 through 2025: long rate locks, steep penalties and little flexibility. That strategy is breaking down in a tighter market, said Craig Lough, director of strategic planning at A. Duie Pyle, who leads the company’s non-asset brokerage division.
Lough has worked in freight since 2003. Pyle is a family-owned carrier based in West Chester, Pennsylvania, that has been expanding its LTL network beyond the Northeast . He said the mismatch is leaving loads uncovered and asking brokers to price more than a year of rate risk into some bids.
The peak season capacity tightness that is invalidating last year’s playbook comes in the form of persistently elevated outbound tender rejection rates. The FreightWaves SONAR Tender Rejection Index held near 13.9% in mid-October, compared with under 6% during peak season 2025, as truckload capacity showed no signs of recovering .
As many of the shippers are still running those playbooks, the routing guide is already bleeding freight, Lough said.
“They’re sticking to the old, ‘You’ve got to sign up long-term, there’s no flexibility,’ but then they’re on the market asking for additional capacity,” he told FreightWaves in an Oct. 8 interview.
Bid terms stretch past a year
Lough has seen bids that lock rates for a month and adjust for fuel, and others that hand brokers lane data five months before go-live, then ask them to hold rates for a year after it.
“So, you’re talking like a 17- to 18-month risk profile in probably either the first or second most volatile market that we’ve seen this century,” he said.
The shippers asking for the longest terms are getting what Lough called paper rates from a good share of the capacity bidding on them.
Lough sorts shippers into two camps: collaboration and consequences. Some shippers open by saying where they need capacity and are struggling. Others lead with fines. He described one bid that opened with a 98% tender acceptance expectation and a $1,000 fine for late delivery.
Other bids remove providers from the routing guide if they decline freight below a set threshold.
“What works in a falling market is a giant red flag in a tightening point,” Lough said.
Some shippers accept weaker service for lower prices
Price-focused shippers are showing a higher pain tolerance, trading weaker service from other providers for lower prices, Lough said. Some may have locked their own customers into full-year prices built on old freight costs before the market flipped.
Pyle has priced loads on a Monday that a shipper wanted moved that day, then seen the same load still posted by other brokers Tuesday and Wednesday, he said.
Quote requests arrive without lane details
Lough has seen more rate requests from shippers Pyle’s brokerage has never spoken with, often with no interest in a discovery call about shipping hours, consignees or delivery windows. When he asked for more information, some stopped responding.
“I think you have some supply chain professionals that started in a loose market and haven’t really had those collaborative conversations before,” he said.
Small carriers that miss standards seek freight
In the three weeks before the interview, Lough said, small carriers had been contacting Pyle “left and right” asking to haul its freight, and they did not pass its standards.
He read that as a sign that other companies had tightened their carrier standards and pushed that capacity back onto the market. Enforcement is also pulling drivers out: English-language proficiency enforcement puts about 2,700 drivers out of service a month, according to FreightWaves SONAR data .
“The fact that these carriers are coming out of the woodwork, to me, that means somebody somewhere, and probably multiple companies, have tightened their standards and started to force this capacity back onto the market. So, in essence, I almost think that there’s two markets that are going on right now,” Lough said.
Pyle is seeing significant pricing premiums into areas with traditionally heavier enforcement, he said. Pricing tools don’t capture them, because Pyle’s carrier standards cost more on those lanes.
Pyle pairs long-term carriers with spot capacity
Pyle moves part of its freight on carriers locked in for extended time periods, Lough said.
“We have some lanes that carriers have been running for us for eight years,” he said.
Pyle also moves spot freight , and some carriers make a living playing that market. Some brokers don’t like those carriers.
“To me, as long as they have the correct standards and they’re a good qualified carrier, they serve a vital part of the market because at the end of the day, whoever needs the truck the most is going to pay that carrier the most and ultimately get it moved,” he said.
Carriers with strong reputations are not hauling at the prices they took two or three years ago, Lough said.
Advice for shippers heading into peak
Lough said relationships are absolutely key.
Lough’s advice for shippers before peak starts with phone calls, video meetings and in-person visits with carriers and brokers, centered on service and capacity. A lot of shippers are still talking about price, he said, but the conversations should also include service and capacity. “We understand price is important, but if you’re sending out lists of loads every day at 11 o’clock in the morning that aren’t covered, what are you going to do here?” he said.
He has also pitched a transparent cost-plus model, in which Pyle shows a shipper what it pays the carrier and adds a markup. If a shipper is targeting $1,000, the broker can report back on whether that price works or if the market is demanding $1,200 or $1,300. No shipper has taken it yet, he said.
“In a fluctuating market where a shipper is wondering, ‘Am I getting a good deal or not?’ If you actually trust a partner to do that cost-plus type model, that could be very advantageous, or you can work together.”
Lough warned against blast emails to lists of about 50 carriers and shippers, because recipients see 50 other people going after the load, and in tight markets those lists get less attention. A couple of months before the interview, he saw a single lane from Baltimore to a remote New England location posted 41 times by 27 brokers on load boards. He wrote about it on LinkedIn and called it an extreme example.
Even three or four brokers on one load can mislead a shipper, he said. Carriers call each broker in turn, and each broker brings the shipper a slightly higher number. In Lough’s example, a shipper who holds out until 3 p.m. finds that the truck offered at $1,100 that morning now wants $1,400.
“In reality, it’s just the same truck making offers to four brokers,” Lough said.
Lough wants shippers talking with carriers and brokers before Thanksgiving. Northeast freight gets harder every year from then until January, he said, as winter weather stacks on top of peak demand.
“If you have that human relationship and are having the conversation, that carrier or broker is probably going to be more likely to say, ‘You know what, I’m going to go ahead and accept this load instead of taking another one from a different provider,'” he said.
Why it matters: Shippers that bid long and price tight are betting capacity returns before their contracts reprice. With enforcement still pulling drivers out of service, that bet pushes freight onto the spot market , where duplicate postings and late-day quotes raise what they pay.

Dealer Visits Seller's House To Buy Six Cars, Picks One for Himself
34 photos
Photo: George J Saliba | YouTube
A senior driver called a dealer and invited him to his house to sell him his car collection. He has an impressive and exclusive lineup of Porsche cars, a DeLorean, a couple of Dodge Challengers, and a Mercedes-Benz. However, things don’t go according to plan, and the dealer ends up with just one car that he is not even planning to sell.
Dealership owner George J. Saliba got a message from a senior car enthusiast who had just sold his business and was planning to downsize his car collection. He offered him a 2018 Dodge Challenger with just 61 miles, a 2016 Challenger Hellcat with 8,400 miles, a 2003 Mercedes-Benz 500 SL with 22,000 miles, and a 1982 DeLorean DMC-12 with just 600 miles.
The pack also includes two very exclusive Porsche models. Charles, the senior car enthusiast, owns a 2014 Porsche Panamera Turbo S Executive Exclusive Series with just 600 miles on the clock, and a 2011 Porsche 911 Turbo S with 4,912 miles and a manual transmission.
So George J Saliba is traveling to Pennsylvania in his Cybertruck, with the FSD on. He is planning to make an offer for all of them. One number for all cars. He is thinking that $295,000 for five of them, without the DeLorean, would make a good offer. But negotiating with Charles is like pulling teeth.
Photo: George J Saliba | YouTube When he offers $55,000 for the Panamera Executive Exclusive Series , both father and son nod their heads in disagreement. They were considering roughly $300,000 for the car, and they are not entirely wrong to do so. The Panamera Executive Exclusive is one of only 100 examples that saw the light of day after the official unveiling at the 2014 Los Angeles Auto Show.
The entire production run was sold out within 48 hours of the official announcement despite the quite hefty price. Porsche asked a starting price of $263,900. But you know, cars start losing value the moment they drive off the showroom floor, and German luxury sports models are the most unfortunate when it comes to depreciation.
Nowadays, such cars command between $80,000 and $125,000 on the used car market, depending on mileage and condition. The Panamera Turbo S Executive Exclusive Series came with Porsche's 4.8-liter twin-turbocharged V8, which pumps out 562 horsepower (570 metric horsepower) and 553 pound-feet (750 Newton meters) of torque.
That is enough to make it rocket from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 3.5 seconds and top out at 193 mph (310 kph). A dual-clutch seven-speed PDK automatic transmission puts the power down through all four corners. Porsche's first four-door rides on 20-inch Sport Classic wheels with bright yellow calipers, clamping Porsche Ceramic Composite Brakes.
Photo: George J Saliba | YouTube A two-tone graduated paintwork, with the Deep Jet Black Metallic covering the upper half and Chestnut Brown Metallic on the lower section, matches the completely bespoke interior in premium Agatha Chestnut Brown leather sourced directly from the renowned Italian luxury furniture house Poltrona Frau.
But that is not the Porsche that impresses George J Saliba the most. For him, it is love at first sight when he lays his eyes on a Porsche 911 Turbo S, finished in black over a red leather interior. If it is the variant with the Mezger engine , as George says it is, then the 3.6-liter twin-turbocharged flat-six puts down 444 horsepower (450 metric horsepower) and 457 pound-feet (620 Newton meters) of torque.
This Porsche can do 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 3.9 seconds on its way to a top speed of 191 mph (307 kph). And, the best part of all, it is a car with a six-speed manual. With that spec and the stick shift, it can't get any better than this, so George is planning to fight for it. The 997.2 Turbo S never came with a manual or a Mezger engine.
" If I'm buying this car, I'm keeping it ," George says. But the owner is asking for over $200,000 for the thing. He offers $91,000 on the Demon. For the whole collection, leaving the DeLorean, the Mercedes, and the 911 out, he can offer $319,000, on top of the $185,000 that he is willing to pay for the 911. The owner says he needs to think. He wants auction prices for his cars without having to go through the actual auction, so he lets George leave empty-handed and waiting for his call.
Photo: George J Saliba | YouTube Days later, George calls first because he is anxious to know if he can make that black 2011 Porsche. 911 Turbo S with a red interior, his own. But the owner is well aware that he wants it badly, so he sets a prohibitive price for the car. He is asking $250,000 for it alone. They eventually close the deal for the 911 only at $220,000. But the other cars remain in the owner's garage. A very demanding owner.
He checks with Grok and raises his fist in the air. Cars like that can hit $300,000 at auctions. However, he plans to keep it. So it is a good deal after all, even if he had to stretch far more than he originally planned. He isn't even sure if the car runs and drives.
The good news is that the engine fires up with no hesitation whatsoever, so on his way back to the dealership, the new owner drives the Porsche and leaves his cameraman with the Cybertruck.

Lucid Motors reported the third-quarter financial results amid an operational reset under new CEO Silvio Napoli. The EV startup has reported a 30% reduction in cash consumption, while also securing $1.75 billion in funding from its Saudi investors. This comes in clutch as CEO Napoli admitted Lucid lost sales because they couldn't figure out "where cars were."
Lucid Motors reported another quarter of heavy losses , with a net loss of $831 million. Thanks to massive cuts and adjustments made since Silvio Napoli was appointed CEO in June, the cash hemorrhage was cut by 30%, to just under $1 billion during the quarter. All in all, a good result in the struggle to stay afloat and bring the Cosmos compact EV to market.
However, the biggest achievement might not be cutting losses, but getting new money to cover current expenses. Lucid secured another $1.75 billion in financial support from Saudi's Public Investment Fund (PIF), its majority shareholder. This comes after the startup raised another $1 billion in April, with $550 million coming from PIF.
PIF is estimated to own about two-thirds of Lucid Motors, and thus is very interested in not wiping out its investment. This explains why it continues to plug the company's holes with cash, even though it sometimes feels like throwing good money after bad. Besides investments, PIF has also offered $2.1 billion in loans throughout 2026. This raises the total funding and additional borrowing capacity to about $4.9 billion in 2026 alone.
This money makes Lucid Motors confident that it will have enough to fund its operations and investments into the fourth quarter of 2027. That should be enough to start Cosmos production, although its success is paramount for the company's survival. The time is also of the essence for the new management team led by CEO Silvio Napoli to get the ins and outs of running a car company.
That's not trivial, as Napoli himself admitted during the third-quarter earnings call. Lucid's CEO said that the carmaker lost sales over the summer, as the company "did not even know where the cars were." This caused significant delivery delays, which led to potential buyers walking away. For a carmaker with thousands of unsold vehicles that's struggling to survive, that's a stark admission.
Silvio Napoli promised this situation has been solved thanks to a new commercial team. Lucid now has better visibility on inventory and logistics and can better estimate when they can deliver the vehicle to a customer. In the third quarter, Lucid was forced to cut production to deal with the bloated inventory. Things should be much better in the fourth quarter.
How much better is anyone's guess. Lucid Motors builds excellent cars, even though they have sometimes been plagued by software bugs. However, they are expensive, luxury products, with prices in the upper five-figure territory, which explains the low sales. The low production numbers make it almost impossible for Lucid to sell its cars profitably. This should ease with the launch of the Cosmos EV in the second half of 2027.

This biggest news of the past week was undoubtedly the revelation of tumors developing in patients with spinal muscular atrophy who received Novartis’ Zolgensma. The FDA has now launched an investigation into the approved gene therapy.
Then, to add insult to injury, the Swiss pharma revealed detailed results from its failed HORIZON cardiovascular trial , and no matter which way the data were cut, the results remained negative. Novartis and partner Ionis revealed in September that pelacarsen, which lowers levels of lipoprotein(a), failed to show efficacy in lowering the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events. With the new data offering “little silver lining,” according to Truist Securities, Lp(a) as a target in cardiovascular disease is being further scrutinized.
On a global scale, China has been on the rise when it comes to biotech, as evidenced by the volume of licensing deals going to Chinese companies. The Asian country has been working toward this goal for a long time, with the government releasing carefully curated strategic plans every five years for the past few decades. Now, the Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO) has released a proposal laying out seven policies the U.S. government can work on to help protect the American biotech industry.
In the weight loss space, the FDA is requiring a label update for all 12 GLP-1 receptor agonists currently on the market to now include a potential increased risk for a rare eye disease that causes optic nerve swelling and can lead to blindness. Cases of the disease have been reported for all currently marketed GLP-1s, according to the FDA, including Novo’s semaglutide drugs Wegovy and Ozempic and Eli Lilly’s tirzepatide franchise, Zepbound and Mounjaro, as well as its oral GLP-1, Foundayo.
On the oral front, frontrunners Novo and Lilly have been duking it out for market share. In its third quarter earnings call last week, Novo said Lilly’s claim that Foundayo is closing on in the Wegovy pill isn’t quite right. Meanwhile, Lilly released results from a Phase 3 sleep apnea trial of Foundayo—upon which the company will seek its second approval in the indication; Lilly’s first sleep apnea approval—and the first overall for the condition—was for its injectable Zepbound in 2024.
Meanwhile, Zealand and Boehringer Ingelheim are one step closer to global regulatory filings for their dual glucagon and GLP-1 receptor agonist survodutide after a late-stage trial showed the drug did not raise the risk of cardiovascular death.
The FDA has a full docket this month, including pending decisions for Summit Therapeutics and Akeso’s bispecific antibody ivonescimab, Capricor’s Duchenne muscular dystrophy cell therapy deramiocel and Vertex’s povetacicept in IgA nephropathy.
Finally, check out BioSpace ’s 2027 Best Places to Work list , which includes Vertex and 49 other life sciences employers.

Forwarders should beware of confusing demand for complex, high-value pharmaceutical therapies with expectations of increased volumes or improved profitability, warned Pharma.Aero secretary general Frank van Gelder this week.
He told The Loadstar that the days of assuming higher-value goods were a free pass to slap the shipper with higher rates were now in the past.
He said shippers now wanted proof that logistics operators can handle specialist medications and time-sensitive treatments.
“Demand for complex, high-value and time-sensitive therapies can increase, even when traditional tonnage grows more slowly or shifts between modes,” he explained. “Operators must demonstrate what their services actually protect.
“This means showing product integrity, continuity of treatment, predictability. and lower total risk. Premium prices cannot be justified merely by applying a pharma label. Profitability will depend on specialisation, measurable quality, and intelligent cost management.”
Instead, Mr van Gelder said, profitability depended on operators having the ability to develop specialist capabilities, demonstrate measurable quality, and manage costs effectively – particularly as pharma logistics requires investment in qualified infrastructure, handling, and personnel.
For forwarders, that distinction is important, because in pharma the requirements of different products can vary considerably, and the costs of maintaining appropriate handling standards can be substantial.
Mr van Gelder said profitability would depend on “specialisation, measurable quality, and intelligent cost management”, adding that the sector faced a broader challenge of balancing investment with the need to maintain affordable healthcare and access to new treatments.
He labelled this the “healthcare pressure point”, with pharmaceutical innovation on one side and affordability, access, and rising costs on the other.
And he noted that the challenge was “not simply whether we can transport the next generation of medicines”, it had become “whether we can help make them accessible and affordable to patients”.
